steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write a short introduction for our paper on assessing neural network robustness to image corruptions over a continuous range, compared against human performance. Motivate the problem with existing robustness evaluations, then present our new concept, metrics, human study, main findings and released resources.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Why corruption robustness matters, and why compare with humans
2. Human vs NN robustness: limits of fixed-parameter evaluations
3. Contributions and outlook

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivation
- corruption robustness essential for NNs in safety-critical domains
- NNs automate tasks done by humans -> compare model robustness with humans

2. Human VS NN robustness
- corruption robustness = average-case performance of NN or humans on a set of image corruption functions
- existing studies (out-of-distribution anomalies, benchmarking, comparison with humans): pre-selected, fixed transformation parameter values for degrees of corruption
- parameter values don't capture how human perception is affected
- example: same brightening parameter -> objects harder to see on bright image, opposite on dark image
- humans perceive/generalize across wide, continuous spectrum, subtle to completely distorted
- preset values -> incomplete coverage -> potentially biased evaluation vs humans

3. Contributions and Outlook
- new concept: visually-continuous corruption robustness (VCR), continuous range of corruption levels
- two human-aware metrics: HMRI, MRSI
- experiments: 7,718 human participants, Mechanical Turk, 14 common image transformations, three sources
- finding: significant robustness gap remains; no model matches humans over entire range (accuracy + prediction consistency); few exceed humans only by small margin at specific levels
- insights on accuracy, degrees of visual corruption, consistency of classification for humans and SoTA NNs
- classes of transformations with similar human robustness (e.g. different noise types) but different NN reactions -> lower cost of measuring human robustness, explain human/model differences
- open-sourced human data as benchmark + Python code for test set generation, testing, retraining

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
For Neural Networks (NN) to be used in safety-critical domains, it is essential that they are robust against corruption that can happen during deployment (i.e., corruption robustness). NN models in these domains automate tasks that humans usually do, so we need to compare the model's robustness with the robustness of humans.

Human VS NN robustness. Corruption robustness measures how well an NN or humans perform on average on a set of image corruption functions. Existing studies, for example on out-of-distribution anomalies, benchmarking, and comparison with humans, usually evaluate robustness against a fixed set of transformation parameter values that are chosen in advance to represent different degrees of image corruption. But parameter values cannot accurately represent how much human perception is affected by image corruptions. For example, if you use the same parameter to brighten an image that is already bright, the objects get harder to see, but on a dark image it has the opposite effect. Also, humans can perceive and generalize across a wide and continuous spectrum of visual corruptions, from subtle to completely distorted. If test sets only use preset parameter values, they could cover the full range of visual corruptions incompletely, and the evaluation could be biased and not accurately represent NN robustness compared with humans.

Contributions and Outlook
- new concept: visually-continuous corruption robustness (VCR), continuous range of corruption levels
- two human-aware metrics: HMRI, MRSI
- 7,718 human participants, Mechanical Turk, 14 common image transformations, three sources
- significant gap remains: no model matches humans across whole range (accuracy + consistency); few exceed humans by small margin at specific levels
- insights on accuracy, degrees of corruption, classification consistency (humans vs SoTA NNs)
- transformation classes where humans similar (e.g. noise types) but NNs differ -> cheaper human measurement, explain differences
- open-sourced human data benchmark + Python code (test set generation, testing, retraining)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
For Neural Networks (NN) to be used in safety-critical domains, it is essential that they are robust against corruption that can happen during deployment (i.e., corruption robustness). NN models in these domains automate tasks that humans usually do, so we need to compare the model's robustness with the robustness of humans.

Human VS NN robustness. Corruption robustness measures how well an NN or humans perform on average on a set of image corruption functions. Existing studies, for example on out-of-distribution anomalies, benchmarking, and comparison with humans, usually evaluate robustness against a fixed set of transformation parameter values that are chosen in advance to represent different degrees of image corruption. But parameter values cannot accurately represent how much human perception is affected by image corruptions. For example, if you use the same parameter to brighten an image that is already bright, the objects get harder to see, but on a dark image it has the opposite effect. Also, humans can perceive and generalize across a wide and continuous spectrum of visual corruptions, from subtle to completely distorted. If test sets only use preset parameter values, they could cover the full range of visual corruptions incompletely, and the evaluation could be biased and not accurately represent NN robustness compared with humans.

Contributions and Outlook. To address this problem, we propose a new concept called visually-continuous corruption robustness (VCR). This concept is about the robustness of neural networks (NN) against a continuous range of image corruption levels. We also introduce two new human-aware NN evaluation metrics (HMRI and MRSI) for assessing NN robustness compared to human performance. We ran extensive experiments with 7,718 human participants on the Mechanical Turk platform, on 14 commonly used image transformations from three different sources. When we compared NN and human VCR with our metrics, we found that there is still a significant robustness gap between NNs and humans: no model fully matches human performance over the entire continuous range in terms of both accuracy and prediction consistency, and only a few models exceed humans, and only by a small margin, at specific levels of corruption. Our experiments also give insights about the robustness of humans and state-of-the-art (SoTA) NNs with respect to accuracy, degrees of visual corruption, and consistency of classification, and these can help develop NNs that match or surpass human perception. We also found classes of corruption transformations where humans had similar robustness (e.g., different types of noise) but NNs reacted differently. Recognizing these classes can help reduce the cost of measuring human robustness and explain the differences between humans and computational models. To help future research, we open-sourced all the human data as a comprehensive benchmark, along with Python code for test set generation, testing, and retraining.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
For Neural Networks (NN), achieving robustness against possible corruption that may be encountered during deployment (i.e., corruption robustness) is essential for applying NN models in safety-critical domains [1]. Since NN models in these domains automate tasks typically performed by humans, it is necessary to compare the model’s robustness with that of humans.

Human VS NN robustness. Corruption robustness measures the average-case performance of an NN or of humans on a set of image corruption functions [1]. Existing studies, including out-of-distribution anomalies [2], benchmarking [1,3], and comparison with humans [4,5], generally evaluate robustness against a pre-selected, fixed set of transformation parameter values representing varying degrees of image corruption. However, parameter values cannot accurately represent the degree to which image corruptions affect human perception. For instance, using the same parameter to brighten an already bright image makes the objects harder to see, but has the opposite effect on a dark image [4]. Additionally, humans can perceive and generalize across a wide and continuous spectrum of visual corruptions, from subtle to completely distorted [6,7]. Relying only on preset parameter values for test sets could therefore lead to incomplete coverage of the full range of visual corruptions, resulting in a potentially biased evaluation that cannot accurately represent NN robustness compared with humans.

Contributions and Outlook. To address this problem, we propose a new concept called visually-continuous corruption robustness (VCR), which focuses on the robustness of neural networks (NN) against a continuous range of image corruption levels. We also introduce two novel human-aware NN evaluation metrics (HMRI and MRSI) to assess NN robustness relative to human performance. We conducted extensive experiments with 7,718 human participants on the Mechanical Turk platform, covering 14 commonly used image transformations from three different sources. Comparing NN and human VCR with our metrics, we found that a significant robustness gap between NNs and humans still exists: no model fully matches human performance across the entire continuous range in terms of both accuracy and prediction consistency, and few models exceed humans, and only by a small margin, at specific levels of corruption. Our experiments also yield insights about the robustness of humans and state-of-the-art (SoTA) NNs regarding accuracy, degrees of visual corruption, and consistency of classification, which can contribute to developing NNs that match or surpass human perception. We also discovered classes of corruption transformations for which humans showed similar robustness (e.g., different types of noise) while NNs reacted differently. Recognizing these classes can help reduce the cost of measuring human robustness and elucidate the differences between humans and computational models. To foster future research, we open-sourced all human data as a comprehensive benchmark, together with Python code that enables test set generation, testing, and retraining.
